chapter_title: Setting Up Go and Node.js Development Environments
chapter_summary:
With Docker and Docker Compose ready, our next step is to prepare the programming language environments that Hyperledger Fabric chaincode and client applications commonly use: Go and Node.js. While Fabric supports other languages like Java, Go and Node.js are the most prevalent and are extensively used in the official samples and community projects. A properly configured environment for these languages is crucial for writing, compiling, and deploying your smart contracts (chaincode) and interacting with your blockchain network.

Let's begin with **Go**. Go is often the language of choice for performance-critical chaincode due to its compilation to native binaries and concurrency features. To install Go, you should download the official binary distribution for your operating system from the golang.org website. For Linux and macOS, this typically involves extracting a tarball to `/usr/local` and then setting up environment variables. For Windows, there's an MSI installer. After installation, the most critical configuration step for Go is setting the `GOPATH` environment variable. `GOPATH` defines your workspace. It's where Go looks for source code, installed packages, and compiled binaries. A common practice is to set `GOPATH` to a directory in your home folder, for example, `~/go` on Linux/macOS or `C:\Users\YourUser\go` on Windows.
```bash
# For Linux/macOS: Add these lines to your shell profile (e.g., ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc)
export GOPATH=$HOME/go
export PATH=$PATH:$GOPATH/bin:/usr/local/go/bin # Ensure Go binaries are in PATH
```
After adding these lines, remember to `source` your profile file (e.g., `source ~/.bashrc`) or restart your terminal. The `/usr/local/go/bin` part ensures the `go` command itself is found, while `$GOPATH/bin` is where Go installs executables from `go install` or `go get`. A common mistake is forgetting to add `$GOPATH/bin` to your `PATH`, which means Go tools or compiled chaincode binaries won't be found by your shell. Always verify your Go installation and `GOPATH` by running `go version` and `echo $GOPATH` (or `echo %GOPATH%` on Windows).

Next, we'll set up **Node.js**. Node.js is excellent for building client applications that interact with your Fabric network, and it's also a popular choice for chaincode development, especially for developers already familiar with JavaScript. The recommended way to install Node.js is by using a version manager like `nvm` (Node Version Manager) for Linux/macOS or `nvm-windows` for Windows. Version managers are invaluable because different Fabric projects or chaincode might require specific Node.js versions. `nvm` allows you to easily install, switch between, and manage multiple Node.js versions.
```bash
# For Linux/macOS: Install nvm (check official nvm GitHub for latest install script)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.1/install.sh | bash
# After nvm installation, close and reopen your terminal.
# Then install a Node.js LTS version (e.g., 16)
nvm install 16
nvm use 16
nvm alias default 16 # Set this as the default version
# Verify Node.js and npm
node --version
npm --version
```
If you prefer not to use a version manager, you can download the official Node.js installer directly from nodejs.org. The installer usually includes `npm` (Node Package Manager), which is essential for managing Node.js project dependencies. Ensure you install an LTS (Long Term Support) version, as these are more stable and recommended for production environments. After installation, verify with `node --version` and `npm --version`.

When working with Hyperledger Fabric, especially with chaincode, be mindful of the Go and Node.js versions specified in the Fabric documentation or sample projects. While Fabric generally supports a range of versions, using a significantly older or newer version than recommended can sometimes lead to unexpected compilation issues or runtime errors. Always check the Fabric release notes for supported language versions. For instance, if a Fabric release specifies Go 1.14+, using Go 1.20 might introduce subtle incompatibilities if your chaincode or dependencies are not fully forward-compatible. Taking the time to properly configure these environments now will ensure a smooth development experience as we delve into writing and deploying chaincode.

screens.title: Setting Up Go and Node.js Development Environments
screens.subtitle: Install, configure, verify, and manage versions for chaincode and client tooling

narration.text: In this chapter we prepare the two most common developer environments used with Hyperledger Fabric: Go and Node. js. You will learn not only how to install the runtimes, but how to configure crucial environment variables, verify installations, and manage versions safely so your chaincode and client applications compile and run reliably. The practical focus is on setting GOPATH and PATH for Go, and using a version manager for Node. js so you can switch LTS releases when a project requires a different runtime. A correctly configured environment prevents simple but time-consuming errors, like "command not found" or mismatched runtime versions that break builds. We'll walk through terminal commands, show the minimal edits you need in your shell profile, and present verification steps you can use to confirm success. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to install each runtime, check versions, and understand why Fabric projects often specify a narrow range of supported language versions. Think about a chaincode sample that fails to compile; the root cause is often an environment mismatch. Keeping that in mind will guide your troubleshooting as you practice the lab.

keyIdea.text: A correct Go and Node.js setup prevents compilation errors and runtime issues when developing and deploying Fabric chaincode and client apps.

screens.title: Installing Go: binaries, tarball, and installers
screens.subtitle: Download the official distribution and place binaries where the shell can find them

narration.text: Installing Go starts with obtaining the official binary distribution for your operating system and placing it where the system can execute the go command. On Linux and Mac O S this commonly means extracting the tarball to /usr/local so that the go executable resides in /usr/local/go/bin. On Windows you typically use the MSI installer which places the binaries into Program Files and updates system-wide entries. After the files are in place, the critical step is to ensure the go binary path is present in your PATH environment variable. If you forget this, the shell cannot find the go command even though files exist on disk. A concrete example: on a Mac O S laptop you might run tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.16.7. darwin-amd64. tar. gz and then add /usr/local/go/bin to PATH in ~/. zshrc. A common misconception is expecting the installer to always set GOPATH for you; it does not. GOPATH is separate: it's your workspace and you typically set it to a directory like ~/go. After installation, run go version to verify the runtime is available. As a takeaway, treat the binary placement and PATH edits as a single atomic step and verify immediately so you avoid later build confusion.

keyIdea.title: Install and expose
keyIdea.text: Place Go binaries in system locations and ensure /usr/local/go/bin (or installed path) is in PATH so the go command is discoverable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Installing Go
Installation steps (Linux/macOS)
Extract the tarball to /usr/local and make sure /usr/local/go/bin is added to PATH.
# Example: extract a tarball on Linux/macOS
sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.16.7.linux-amd64.tar.gz
# Then add to your shell profile
export PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin
Note: The installer typically does not set GOPATH. Set GOPATH yourself to a workspace like $HOME/go.
Verify: run go version and expect a version string to appear.
Installation steps (Windows)
Use the MSI installer. Then set a system GOPATH and add %GOPATH%\bin to the Path environment variable if needed.
# Verify Go on Windows (CMD)
go version
echo %GOPATH%
Key Takeaway

Installation must be followed by PATH updates and verification commands to avoid invisible runtime errors.

screens.title: GOPATH and the Go workspace
screens.subtitle: What GOPATH is and why it matters for chaincode development

narration.text: GOPATH defines a Go workspace: the directory where source code, installed packages, and compiled Go binaries live. In Fabric development, GOPATH matters because when you build or install chaincode and tools, Go places executables into GOPATH/bin by default. A common practice is to set GOPATH to a directory inside your home directory, for example $HOME/go on Linux and Mac O S or C:\Users\YourUser\go on Windows. If you do not add $GOPATH/bin to your PATH, tools installed with go install or go get will not be found by your shell and commands will fail. A concrete example: after setting GOPATH=$HOME/go and exporting PATH=$PATH:$GOPATH/bin:/usr/local/go/bin, running go install github. com/example/tool will create an executable in ~/go/bin that you can run directly. A misconception is thinking GOPATH is a replacement for module-aware builds; modern Go uses modules, but GOPATH remains the default location for installed binaries and for older workflows. As a takeaway, treat GOPATH as your local workspace and ensure its bin directory is visible to the shell so Fabric build tools are discoverable. GOPATH and the Go workspace means gopath is your workspace; add $gopath/bin to path so installed go tools and chaincode binaries are executable.. In practical terms, what gopath is and why it matters for chaincode development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GOPATH essentials
keyIdea.text: GOPATH is your workspace; add $GOPATH/bin to PATH so installed Go tools and chaincode binaries are executable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › GOPATH
Definition

GOPATH points to your Go workspace where source, packages, and installed executables live. It complements but does not replace modules for source management.

Typical setting examples:
# Linux/macOS ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc
export GOPATH=$HOME/go
export PATH=$PATH:$GOPATH/bin:/usr/local/go/bin
# Windows (set as system variable)
# GOPATH = C:\Users\YourUser\go
# add %GOPATH%\bin to Path
Example
After setting GOPATH and PATH, install a tool and run it from the shell.
go install github.com/example/tool@latest
# executable appears in $GOPATH/bin and can be run directly
tool --help
Common mistake: forgetting to export $GOPATH/bin to PATH — tools then appear installed but cannot be run.

screens.title: Verifying Go installation and environment
screens.subtitle: Commands and the expected outputs you should capture

narration.text: Verification is simple but essential. Start by running go version to confirm the go executable resolves correctly and to see the installed version. Next, check your GOPATH with echo $GOPATH on Linux/Mac O S or echo %GOPATH% on Windows. If GOPATH is empty, create and export it. Then confirm that the expected binary directories are present in PATH so your tools will be found. A concrete verification flow: run go version and expect a line such as go version go1.16.7 linux/amd64. If the shell responds with command not found, the PATH is the problem and you should add /usr/local/go/bin to PATH. A common misconception is to assume go env will correct PATH issues; go env prints configuration but does not change your shell. For chaincode workflows, also verify that go env GOPATH prints the same workspace you set. Finally, capture terminal output as proof for assessments. The takeaway is this: verification eliminates guesswork before you attempt to compile chaincode, dramatically reducing troubleshooting time. Verifying Go installation and environment means run go version and echo your gopath immediately after installation to confirm the runtime and workspace are correct.. In practical terms, commands and the expected outputs you should capture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify early

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Verify Go
Verification commands
go version
go env GOPATH
echo $GOPATH
Expected outcomes: go version shows installed version; go env GOPATH and echo $GOPATH return the workspace you set.
Common issues and fixes
  • If go version returns "command not found", add /usr/local/go/bin to PATH and reload your shell.
  • If go env GOPATH differs from your expected workspace, export the desired GOPATH in your profile and source it.
  • Remember to include $GOPATH/bin in PATH so installed executables are runnable.
Key Takeaway

Verifying immediately after install saves time—capture outputs for reproducibility and assessment.

screens.title: A simple Go "hello world" and build check

narration.text: A hands-on way to confirm your Go setup is to create a minimal program, run it, and then build an executable. Start by creating a directory inside your GOPATH or a module-aware directory. For a simple test, create main. go with a basic program that prints a line to stdout. Run the program with go run main. go to exercise the interpreter path, then use go build to produce a binary in the current folder or go install to place it in GOPATH/bin. A concrete example: write a main function that prints "Hello, Fabric". After go build, run the produced binary and observe the output. A common misconception is that module mode removes the need for GOPATH; modules affect source management but the binary install location still matters when you want globally accessible tools. This exercise confirms the runtime, compiler, and PATH behavior together. As a final step, try go install and then run the binary by name to verify $GOPATH/bin visibility. That repeatable cycle—edit, run, build, install, verify—gives you confidence before compiling more complex chaincode. screens.title: Installing Node.js with nvm
screens.subtitle: Use a version manager to install and switch Node LTS releases

narration.text: Installing Node. js with a version manager like nvm gives you flexibility and safety. The recommended flow is to install nvm using the official install script on Linux or Mac O S, then close and reopen the terminal so the nvm command is available. Next, install a Node. js LTS release, for example 16, using nvm install 16. Switch the shell to that runtime with nvm use 16 and optionally set it as the default using nvm alias default 16. Verifying node --version and npm --version confirms both runtime and package manager are present. The practical benefit is this: if a Fabric sample requires a specific Node version, you can switch quickly without global reinstall. A common misconception is that system installers are always superior; they may work, but they make switching versions harder. Using nvm lets you test multiple projects that require different Node versions on the same machine. For Windows, nvm-windows exists as an alternative, or you can use the official installer if you prefer. The takeaway is to adopt a version manager for robust development across Fabric projects.

keyIdea.title: Use a manager
keyIdea.text: nvm installs multiple Node.js versions side-by-side and lets you switch quickly to match project requirements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Install Node.js with nvm
nvm install flow
# Install nvm (check for latest script)
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.1/install.sh | bash
# Then restart the terminal
nvm install 16
nvm use 16
nvm alias default 16
# Verify
node --version
npm --version
Why this matters
  • Switch Node versions quickly to match Fabric samples or project dependencies.
  • Avoid breaking global Node installs when testing multiple projects.
  • nvm isolates versions per shell session, reducing side effects.
Key Takeaway

Prefer nvm on Linux/macOS for safe, flexible Node version management; consider nvm-windows or the installer on Windows.

screens.title: npm and dependency management
screens.subtitle: How npm fits into Fabric client development

narration.text: npm is the default package manager for Node. js and it is essential for managing dependencies in Fabric client applications and JavaScript chaincode. Once Node and npm are available, you use npm to install packages required by your project and to run scripts defined in package. json. A concrete example is installing fabric-network or fabric-client packages using npm install --save package-name inside a project directory. If npm isn't available, package installation fails and your client or chaincode won't run. A common misconception is that npm versions don't matter; in reality, npm version mismatches can affect lockfile formats or behavior during install, which can lead to inconsistent dependency trees. Verifying npm --version after installing Node ensures the package manager is present. When using nvm, npm is tied to each installed Node version, so switching Node versions may switch npm versions too. The takeaway: confirm npm alongside Node and use package. json best practices so your Fabric client dependencies are reproducible and portable. npm and dependency management means npm installs and manages dependencies for node-based fabric clients and chaincode; verify npm after installing node.. After installation, check node_modules and the package.json dependencies to ensure the library was added.
Common pitfall
If npm is missing or the wrong version, installs may fail or produce lockfiles that others cannot reproduce. When switching Node versions with nvm, re-run npm install to ensure native modules match the runtime.
Key Takeaway

Treat npm as part of the runtime; verify it and be mindful that it changes with Node versions managed by nvm.

screens.title: Windows vs Linux/macOS installation differences
screens.subtitle: What to expect when installing on different operating systems

narration.text: The fundamental steps are the same across platforms — install the runtime, update environment variables, and verify — but details differ and those differences matter. On Linux and Mac O S you typically extract a tarball for Go and edit ~/. bashrc or ~/. zshrc to export GOPATH and append /usr/local/go/bin and $GOPATH/bin to PATH. You also use nvm's install script to manage Node versions. On Windows you commonly use MSI installers for Go and the official Node installer, or use nvm-windows for version management. For Windows, GOPATH is set as a system environment variable and %GOPATH%\bin must be added to Path in system settings. A common misconception is that environment edits on one OS can be applied verbatim to another — path separators and profile locations differ, so copy-pasting commands between OSes will often fail. For example, echo $GOPATH works in a Unix shell but echo %GOPATH% is the correct check in Windows CMD. The takeaway is to follow OS-specific instructions and verify with the platform-specific verification commands to ensure the tools work as expected. screens.title: Why version management matters for Fabric
screens.subtitle: Avoid subtle incompatibilities by aligning runtimes with Fabric requirements

narration.text: Version management matters because Fabric releases often document supported language versions and samples are written against specific runtimes. Using an unsupported or significantly different language version can produce subtle compilation differences, dependency misbehavior, or runtime errors. For example, a Fabric release might expect a certain Go minor version or a Node LTS; deviating from that could cause chaincode to fail compilation or libraries to behave differently. A concrete scenario: using a far newer Go version could expose language or dependency changes that older Fabric samples do not expect. A common misconception is that newer is always better; while later versions often fix bugs, they can also change default behaviors that chaincode or dependencies rely on. The safe approach is to consult the Fabric release notes and align your local runtimes. When you use nvm for Node or install explicit Go versions, you can reproduce the environment that the sample or release expects, which simplifies debugging and collaboration across teams. Why version management matters for Fabric means align your go and node.js versions with fabric release notes to avoid compatibility and build issues.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Version Management

  • Use nvm to switch Node versions for different projects without reinstalling globally.
  • Install and test the specified Go version when a sample explicitly references it.
Misconception
Newer language versions will always be compatible. In practice, API changes or module differences can break older code. Match the runtime to the project's expectations.
